Recent studies have demonstrated the potential of using pre-trained language models to generate novel text sequences. However, current techniques often struggle to maintain coherence and natural flow over long periods of time. In response, we have developed a novel approach called LATTE (LAnguage Trajectory TransformEr), which enhances the generation of text sequences by leveraging a technique called optimal transport, thereby enabling the creation of more extended and coherent text contents. Through experimentation with prominent language models such as GPT-2 and XLNet, as well as the evaluation of metrics including BLEU, Measuring Coherence and Naturality and human assessment, LATTE has been shown to outperform traditional methods in generating text sequences of up to 10 times the original length. In particular, LATTE has been shown to improve text coherence by 7.7% and natural flow by 5.4% compared to previous techniques. A detailed analysis of the results also reveals that LATTE's ability to generate more coherent text is due to its capacity to preserve the underlying structure of the original text and transfer this structure to longer sequences. In addition, we have demonstrated the potential of LATTE in generating text summaries by sampling from the generated sequences. A human evaluation has confirmed that LATTE's generated sequences are indeed effective for summarization tasks. Finally, we have demonstrated the potential of LATTE in generating text sequences in multiple languages by leveraging language models that have been trained on multilingual datasets. Through experimentation with a range of languages, LATTE has been shown to be capable of generating coherent and natural flow text contents in multiple languages. Preconditioned eigensolvers are essential tools for solving linear eigenvalue problems, and understanding their convergence rates is vital for optimizing solvers. Although extensive research has been conducted on geometric convergence analysis for specific solvers, such as the power iteration, an in-depth study for preconditioned eigensolvers is still lacking. In this research, a gradient flow framework is employed to analyze geometric convergence for preconditioned eigensolvers. It is demonstrated that geometric convergence rates are achievable in certain cases and a convergence rate estimation is developed for general preconditioned eigensolvers. Additionally, a detailed analysis of geometric convergence for preconditioned Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel iterations is conducted. The findings reveal that these methods can achieve superlinear and even exponential convergence rates under specific conditions. The research provides a comprehensive geometric convergence analysis for a broad range of preconditioned eigensolvers and sheds new light on the convergence rates of these methods. This research paper delves into predicting the occurrence of traffic accidents and
the locations involved on video footage from traffic cameras. Early warning systems
could potentially save lives by alerting drivers to potential hazards, and we aim
to address this challenge. We propose a Dynamic Spatial-Temporal Attention Network
(DSTAN), which leverages both temporal and spatial data for accurate prediction.
The proposed method outperforms existing approaches on various test cases. Notably,
DSTAN displays exceptional performance in anticipating accidents in relatively brief
video clips, and it successfully identifies the precise accident area through its
spatial detection capabilities. Additionally, we demonstrate that the proposed
attention map visually represents the accident scenes that DSTAN predicts. Our
research is the first to anticipate accidents in a timely manner and with greater
precision using a human-like visual attention mechanism. Lastly, we showcase that
DSTAN generalizes its knowledge to similar scenarios, indicating its potential for
practical applications. We will make our code publicly available on GitHub.

In this research, we investigate policy optimization under constraints in
Markov decision processes and establish a new optimization-based approach.
We initially cast the constrained policy optimization issue as a Markov
measurable Markov decision process optimization problem and prove that
its equivalent solution has a polynomial time of $O(\sqrt{k} d L)$ where
$k$, $d$, and $L$ are the number of states, dimensions, and the diameter,
respectively. To tackle this challenge, we introduce a novel algorithm that
utilizes the proximal point method to handle constraints and the
counterfactual regret minimization technique to optimize policies, leading
to a fast convergence rate of $O(\sqrt{k}/L)$ in the absence of constraints.
This research presents a groundbreaking fast convergence rate for policy
optimization under constraints and highlights the critical role of
counterfactual regret minimization in achieving this rate. Furthermore,
our findings are applicable to zero-sum multi-agent settings, resulting in
the first fast convergence rate for Nash equilibrium computation in zero-sum
constrained two-player Markov measurable games. Our theoretical results are
verified through numerical simulations. For more details, please refer to

utilizing an innovative regularization strategy that incorporates sparse prior

sparse GP models with fewer inducing points compared to traditional dense models, 
resulting in substantial computational savings. Furthermore, we show that this 
approach leads to enhanced mass mapping precision and improved convergence rates 
on simulated data containing realistic mass distribution patterns in the 
presence of point-source artifacts. This method is also applied to actual data, 
yielding consistent results that agree with established findings in the literature. 
Our proposed approach is made available as open-source software for further 
utilization. This research highlights the potential of sparse Gaussian process 
regression in producing accurate and efficient weak lensing mass maps.

surrogates for efficient inference in mass mapping problems. These surrogates,

linearly with the number of inducing points used. These neural network models are

In the realm of active learning, a particular strategy known as Performance Improving Query (PIQ) actively seeks out the dataset examples that would most benefit the model by querying them and then retraining the model with these examples. However, existing PIQ methods that aim to enhance the model's performance by selecting the most informative examples often rely on various metrics such as mutual information or the gradient of the loss function, which can sometimes be subjective and lead to suboptimal results due to an overemphasis on information gain. Furthermore, these methods may fail to consider the potential negative impact of introducing noisy labels to the model's performance. To address these limitations, we introduce a new PIQ method called PIQ-Boost, which not only considers the information gain and potential noise, but also leverages a learned noise-aware classifier to guide the query process. As a result, PIQ-Boost is able to identify more informative examples that would lead to better performance for the model. Our experimental results demonstrate that PIQ-Boost outperforms state-of-the-art active learning methods across a range of datasets and models. Additionally, we found that PIQ-Boost exhibits a notable advantage in terms of information gain and noise robustness compared to other PIQ methods. For instance, it outperformed the baseline PIQ method by 1.5% and 1.4% respectively in terms of accuracy on the CIFAR-100 dataset. To monitor the health of individuals in video recordings and ensure their safety during exercise, it is crucial to develop a method for estimating heart rate. However, estimating heart rate can be challenging, especially when the subject is engaged in high-intensity physical activity, such as burpees or push-ups, as it can be difficult to accurately track the heart rate from video footage. To address this issue, we have developed a new method that uses a dataset of 1,381 videos of individuals performing various exercises to train a neural network to estimate heart rate. This dataset, known as ExerDietHeart, is a result of collaboration between researchers from the University of California, Los Angeles, and the University of California, San Diego. By utilizing body pose information and activity data, our method can effectively estimate heart rate, even during intense exercise. This new method has been shown to be effective and efficient, with a processing time of 0.1 seconds, making it a promising solution for real-time heart rate monitoring during exercise. This method combines the advantages of both voxel and region-based models, offering a more robust estimation framework. In contrast to traditional region-based fMRI analyses, which can be biased by low signal quality in less active brain areas, the proposed approach leverages high-quality signals from individual voxels to enhance regional connectivity estimates. This is achieved by integrating voxel-level and region-based data within a mixed-effects model, which allows for the simulation of region-level BOLD signals based on voxel-level data. This model enables the estimation of regional connectivity using a modified maximum likelihood estimation technique. The proposed approach is evaluated through simulation studies and real-world applications, demonstrating its potential to provide more accurate and biologically meaningful estimates of functional connectivity by capitalizing on the strengths of both voxel and region-based fMRI analyses. A common data analysis strategy using sequential regression models, known as multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE), allows researchers to analyze incomplete data by iteratively filling in missing values using different models in each step. Typically, each model in the chain is fitted with a simple linear regression, which can lead to biased estimates if there are many missing values, especially if there are a large number of variables. Building on previous research, we suggest a more robust approach to addressing this issue and evaluate its performance on simulated data. This new strategy involves using principal component regression, which can handle multiple variables without significantly increasing the risk of overfitting. Our results show that this approach produces more accurate predictions compared to traditional methods, especially when there are many missing values, leading to reduced type I errors. We demonstrate that this improvement applies to other statistical models used in MICE cycles, such as logistic regression, generalized linear models, and survival analysis. Consequently, we recommend using principal component regression as the default method in MICE cycles, especially when there are many missing values or a large number of variables. Additionally, we suggest considering a more conservative approach to data analysis, such as reducing the sample size, when there are many missing values and many variables, which can lead to biased estimates. Overall, our research highlights the importance of addressing the "many variables" problem in MICE, which can lead to biased estimates and type I errors. We hope that our findings will motivate further research to develop more robust methods for addressing this issue. Recent breakthroughs in natural language processing have been largely driven by
pre-trained language models. However, these models' limitations in tasks such as
common sense reasoning and practical problem-solving have become increasingly
apparent. To address this issue, researchers have been exploring methods to
enhance language model capabilities by incorporating additional knowledge. This
paper presents an innovative approach to achieving this goal by linking
language model outputs to specific, measurable properties. This breakthrough enables
the development of a groundbreaking semantic grounding framework, which can be
used to verify and expand the capabilities of pre-trained language models. To
demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework, we have integrated a
semantically driven semantic classifier into the BART language model and tested
it on a range of tasks, including identifying real-world events in text and
extracting relevant information. Our results show that this enhanced model
significantly outperforms the original BART in these challenging tasks, with
improvements of 10.2% in event detection and 8.7% in question answering. Moreover, 
the framework allows for the identification of specific areas where the model
needs further improvement. All the necessary code and data are publicly available. 
This development marks a significant milestone in bridging the gap between
language models and human understanding. Ultimately, our long-term goal is to
develop a language model that can be used to reason and solve real-world problems.

This study presents an efficient method for improving the performance of deep learning-based semantic segmentation in remote sensing images. The approach involves an iterative process combining supervised learning with interactive and active techniques. Initially, a segmentation model is trained using a limited number of samples from a remote sensing image, and then a human annotator interacts with the output to indicate areas in need of correction. Subsequently, additional samples are generated from the corrected output and incorporated into the training dataset for further improvement. This iterative process continues until the performance of the segmentation model reaches an acceptable level or until a pre-defined stopping point is reached. Experimental results from three distinct datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in improving segmentation results, with significant reductions in training sample requirements. Additionally, the use of active learning was found to enhance performance while reducing sample requirements, with notable benefits observed across a wide range of metrics, including IoU, ACC, and F1-score. Complex Bayesian models can be computationally expensive to analyze, making it necessary to utilize simpler, yet more reliable approximate methods for large datasets. In particular, Gaussian processes are often too computationally demanding, making the Simplified Laplace approximation a more viable option for approximate Bayesian inference in latent Gaussian models. This method, which builds on the INLA approach, provides a more efficient solution, especially when exact GP models are impractical. To further enhance its capabilities, we introduce an extension to the Laplace approximation, the Extended Simplified Laplace, by incorporating a key modification to the INLA algorithm. This modification enables the ESL to effectively handle complex distributions, including those with non-standard parameters, and even those that do not meet specific conditions. To illustrate its utility, we apply the ESL to three distinct datasets: a univariate mixed effects model, a multivariate model, and a model assessing the effect of meteorological factors on malaria transmission. The results suggest that the ESL offers a reliable, more general solution for approximating Bayesian inference in a wide range of latent Gaussian models. In reinforcement learning, model-free approaches have seen success in various domains, but often struggle with generalization across different settings. To address this issue, we introduce Temporal Shift Reinforcement Learning (TSRL), which enables agents to produce shift-agnostic policies. TSRL achieves this by training an agent on multiple environments simultaneously and encouraging it to adapt its actions based on changing environmental shifts over time. TSRL employs a multi-task deep learning architecture, which includes a feature extractor and two policy networks. The feature extractor is trained to capture general features across all environments, while the policy networks learn to adapt to temporal shifts using shift-specific representations. To promote shift invariance, a shift consistency loss function is added to the TSRL objective. TSRL is demonstrated to be effective in various multi-environment reinforcement learning scenarios, including image classification, robotic tasks, and game-based MDPs. This study examines the connection between various engagement methods and participation rates in EU Code Week. By analyzing two years of Code Week data, our research reveals a strong link between the distribution strategy and the overall enrollment numbers. Specifically, schools with higher enrollment numbers tend to adopt multiple code-learning approaches. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that a key Code Week goal may be difficult to achieve: encouraging schools to adopt a single code-learning method, as diverse methods are often used concurrently. These findings provide valuable insights for policy makers, educators, and stakeholders involved in digital education initiatives. Yet, our research also identifies some limitations in the current data available, such as a lack of information on the specific age ranges and geographical regions or the implementation of digital technologies used during events. Researchers in neural architecture search have developed methods to analyze large collections of neural network designs in order to identify effective design strategies for creating intelligent models. Although previous studies have explored various metrics, they primarily focus on individual characteristics of network designs, disregarding the interconnections between them. This research introduces a new method for analyzing vast collections of neural network designs, employing a graph-based representation that captures the relationships between network features. By applying dimension reduction and clustering techniques, we can derive overarching principles to guide the design of intelligent models. Our experiments using a large collection of over 1.1 million network designs demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Our results reveal that network architecture designs can be condensed into a three-dimensional space and that these designs fall into three primary categories. These categories correspond to different network types: small, medium, and large models. Our findings also indicate that network designers tend to focus on certain key network features rather than a broad spectrum, and that network architecture can be improved by combining existing designs. This research demonstrates how graph-based analysis can be employed to identify effective design strategies for creating intelligent models. Our results provide valuable insights for future studies on neural architecture search and analysis. On e-commerce platforms like Lazada, sellers can create sponsored search ads that appear as results for product-related search queries. The cost per click generated by these ads is determined by an auction-based system. To maximize revenue, Lazada aims to strike a balance between encouraging sellers to bid aggressively and providing competitive outcomes to users. To achieve this, Lazada introduced a reserve price strategy that adjusts the minimum price per click. Through extensive testing, the publisher discovered that setting a fixed reserve price results in sellers who are less responsive to market changes, whereas an optimal reserve price that changes according to predicted click values increases seller responsiveness. Lazada's dynamic reserve price approach outperforms the traditional fixed price method, yielding higher revenue and better user experiences. Furthermore, the publisher developed a machine learning model that can predict click values and support the successful implementation of this strategy. By leveraging this model, Lazada's revenue from search increased by 20-30% after adopting the dynamic reserve price. To support further analysis, the paper includes a companion repository with the underlying data and implementation. The repository can be accessed at: https://github.com/ChenyaoGao/competitive-auction. Additional details about the machine learning model can be found in a separate technical report. Lazada's management team has also provided insights on the practical applications of this research in a companion document. In this research, we investigate distributed maximum likelihood estimation with quantized data, focusing on a scenario where multiple Gaussian sources experience a non-linear, time-varying correlation and are then transmitted over an erasure channel. The study explores the impact of quantization on estimation accuracy and, drawing inspiration from recent findings, proposes a novel quantization scheme that accounts for temporal dependence in the Gaussian sources. The new scheme achieves a balance between quantizer design and decoder implementation, resulting in enhanced estimation performance. The theoretical analysis demonstrates that the proposed scheme outperforms existing methods, with simulation results validating these findings and confirming the scheme's resilience to malicious sensor attacks. Furthermore, the simulation outcomes reveal that the proposed scheme offers improved performance over existing state-of-the-art quantization methods. Interestingly, the study also finds that the influence of sensor-sensor dependence on estimation accuracy is contingent on the presence of a time-varying sensor-sensor correlation. When this correlation is present, the proposed scheme enhances performance, whereas its absence degrades performance; however, the latter can be mitigated by adopting a uniform quantizer, which is particularly beneficial in the absence of sensor dependence. Notably, a uniform quantizer is sub-optimal when sensor dependence is present, with the proposed scheme offering a more versatile solution that accommodates both scenarios effectively. Ultimately, the proposed scheme presents a unified framework for designing quantizers that are adaptable to both dependent and independent sensor nodes. In practice, a uniform quantizer is a more straightforward and efficient solution for independent sensor nodes, whereas the proposed scheme excels in the dependent case. The study's findings are also applicable to distributed learning in the context of deep learning, with the proposed scheme facilitating distributed learning via quantized gradient transmission and enabling real-world implementation via a simple threshold quantizer design. Go, a popular open-source concurrent language, lacks static bug detection capabilities in multi-core environments. To bridge this gap, researchers developed BinGo, a fully automated tool that uses binary analysis to identify Go concurrency bugs. By analyzing binary code, BinGo detects Go statements that may lead to concurrency issues such as synchronization errors, data corruption, and the vulnerability to race conditions. Once identifying these problems, it provides detailed explanations and recommendations for resolution. A study involving 1,000 Go programs revealed that BinGo accurately detected 1,000 concurrency bugs, of which 91% were validated by subsequent manual inspections. Further evaluation showed that BinGo outperformed existing tools in both bug detection accuracy and false positive rates, with an average detection time of 1.38 seconds. This study's results are expected to inspire the development of other binary-based concurrency bug detectors for Go applications. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our modified strategy achieves near-optimal outcomes for the zig-zag sequence case as well. In the context of massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems, the use of 1-bit feedback is explored for downlink communication, particularly in scenarios where channel state information (CSI) is incomplete. A novel approach called Bi-Rec 1-bit CSI feedback is introduced, leveraging the bidirectional channel reciprocity found in many wireless systems, allowing for the derivation of downlink CSI from uplink data. However, existing methods for the bidirectional method are limited by their reliance on quantized transceiver information, leading to suboptimal performance. To address this, a new framework called Fusion Learning is proposed, treating quantized transceiver information as a form of weak supervision. This approach allows for the incorporation of external information, such as quantizer coefficients, to improve the accuracy of quantized transceiver information. Furthermore, a novel objective function is designed to optimize the quantized transceiver information, leading to superior performance. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, achieving a significant reduction in error rate of up to 10.3 dB and outperforming existing methods by up to 0.4 dB. Additionally, the proposed method offers improved robustness against noisy external information, maintaining a performance gain of 5.9 dB with limited information. Overall, the proposed method offers a superior alternative to existing methods for the bidirectional method. In human conversations, people often draw upon individualized relationships and prior knowledge when expressing themselves, a phenomenon absent in current computer-based conversations. To address this, we propose the concept of the "customized conversation," where conversational agents tailor their responses based on an individual user's characteristics and knowledge. We introduce a specific task, "customized conversation grounding persona and knowledge," requiring AI models to identify relevant user-specific information from text to inform their responses. We establish a large-scale dataset, Customized Conversation Dataset, featuring 80,000 conversations among 40,000 users. Additionally, we created a specific conversational agent, PAK-PER, that effectively integrates user data and knowledge to produce more individualized responses. Experimental results demonstrate that this model outperforms others in tasks related to understanding user personas and knowledge. PAK-PER's responses are also evaluated as being more human-like than those of leading commercial conversational agents. The associated code and dataset can be found at this GitHub repository: https://github.com/THU-KEG/CCGPK. This research marks a significant step forward in creating conversational agents that engage users in a more personalized manner. We anticipate that this advancement will ultimately lead to more natural and personalized interactions. A primary obstacle hindering the creation of accurate intent predictors lies in the scarcity of annotated developer code. Through experimentation on a dataset of over 1.2 million Java classes, our results indicate that the Observer model surpasses existing approaches in intent prediction by achieving a 7% improvement in the F1 macro score. Additionally, our analysis reveals that the Observer effectively captures intended code snippets from unlabelled code, thus underscoring the importance of this approach for intent prediction. Generative models trained on limited data often struggle to disentangle the components of their input data, which is particularly challenging when working with low-quality, limited, or unlabelled data. To overcome this issue, we propose a novel semi-supervised approach to disentanglement learning, which uses a style-based generative network to identify and separate distinct characteristics of objects, such as their shape and texture. By leveraging the versatility of stylegan, this method enables the simultaneous training on both labelled and unlabelled datasets. Through extensive testing on numerous datasets, our method consistently demonstrates superior performance and robustness compared to existing disentanglement techniques. Additionally, it is shown to be highly effective in generating novel object variations, such as different colours or textures, which holds potential applications in real-world tasks like object manipulation. To enhance the safety and effectiveness of autonomous vehicles through testing, we have developed a new method of generating realistic driving scenarios. These realistic scenarios are designed to capture various driving situations and driver behavior, which can be challenging for autonomous vehicles to encounter. Our approach integrates knowledge of human drivers' behavior and rules of the road directly into the generation process using a technique called knowledge distillation. This method allows us to evaluate the effectiveness of our generated scenarios by comparing the output of a self-driving system to the behavior of human drivers. Our results demonstrate the success of our integrated approach, producing diverse and realistic driving scenarios that simulate the actions of human drivers. These generated scenarios can be used to simulate real-world driving situations, making them an essential tool for improving autonomous vehicle safety. However, traditional approaches to parallelization can lead to suboptimal performance and resource utilization. To address this challenge, we propose a novel distributed RL training framework called distributed dataflow (DDF), which leverages knowledge of RL dataflow to automatically optimize resource allocation. To make DDF training efficient, we represent RL dataflow as a fragment-based language and develop an optimization language (OLANG) to analyze and optimize these fragments. By applying OLANG to DDF training, we demonstrate its ability to outperform existing RL training systems in both efficiency and effectiveness on diverse tasks. Our results show that DDF can reduce training time and energy consumption while achieving comparable results to state-of-the-art RL systems on challenging tasks such as Atari games and D4RL. Reverberation, which distorts speech and limits speech intelligibility, poses significant challenges in multi-speaker, highly reverberant environments. To address this issue, we introduce a novel adaptive scheme that combines a masking component estimator with a non-stationary masking component detector, allowing for enhanced speech intelligibility. This estimator identifies masked components, and an adaptive equalizer adjusts its length to accommodate these elements, thereby improving signal quality. To verify its effectiveness, we conducted extensive experiments on both clean and reverberant child speech signals, yielding substantial improvements in signal quality and intelligibility over existing methods. Notably, our scheme achieves a 4.7 dB increase in signal quality and 2.5% improvement in intelligibility, surpassing competing approaches. Furthermore, its performance is robust, with minimal impact from variations in reverberation time, speaker number, and speech type. When applied to real-world scenarios, our method demonstrates a 3.5 dB signal quality improvement and 2.2% intelligibility boost. Overall, our scheme offers superior signal quality and intelligibility gains compared to prior studies. To facilitate future research, we will make our model and associated code publicly available. Additionally, our research contributes to the development of speech processing systems capable of adapting to multi-speaker, highly reverberant, and non-stationary environments. This paper's primary objective is to analyze specific characteristics of generalized Mathieu power series that converge within the unit disk. It derives and examines inequalities for these series, including a connection made between their coefficients and terms. This relationship leads to conclusions regarding the series' growth patterns and their derivatives. Additionally, necessary conditions for the existence of their partial sums are discussed. We also explore their uniqueness within the context of univalent functions. Specifically, it is proven that the function $f(z)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}c_{n}z^{n+1}$, when conformally invertible, fulfills certain criteria. This conclusion is supported by multiple applications of the two-parameter coefficient problem proposed by Cowling. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the series' growth patterns align with those of functions in the class $\mathcal{B}$ when conformally invertible. Lastly, a few relevant observations are presented as corollaries to these findings. This research extends previous work by Noor, Avazzadeh and Ali in [Noor et al., Bull. Malays. Math. Sci. 40 (2017), 69-81]. It also generalizes and broadens the research by noha et al. in [noha et al., Bull. Malays. Math. Sci. 43 (2018), 763-782]. Additionally, it touches on some results related to the generalized Mathieu power series that converge outside the unit disk. The vast array of datasets available for object detection tasks has led to confusion among researchers, who are struggling to determine the most suitable datasets to use for their specific needs. To address this challenge, we present a novel approach to object detection that involves combining multiple datasets in a more structured manner. Our method utilizes a Faster R-CNN framework to leverage the strengths of different datasets, but we face several challenges in terms of data compatibility, including varying image sizes, object annotations, and annotation formats. To address these issues, we propose a novel data-merging strategy that involves aligning image sizes and annotating objects in a canonical manner, which enables us to create a unified dataset for training. Furthermore, we introduce a soft distillation loss that enables our model to learn from diverse datasets without relying on pixel-wise annotations. The proposed OMNIA Faster R-CNN approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmark datasets, including COCO, VOC, MS-COCO-20k, and MS-COCO-30k, with particularly impressive results on the MS-COCO-20k and MS-COCO-30k benchmarks. Additionally, we demonstrate that our model can adapt to new, unseen datasets and achieve competitive performance within a few iterations of training. The source code for our approach will be made available on GitHub. Overall, we believe that our dataset-merging and soft distillation techniques will be valuable contributions to the object detection community. Reinforcement learning agents often struggle with continuous actions and non-stable tasks. To overcome this challenge, we've developed a universal reinforcement learning method that works across various unstable environments and games by combining elements from proximal policy optimization and policy distillation. This new algorithm, ProxPollo, uses a stable inner policy and a fast outer policy that can adapt quickly to changing conditions. This outer policy learns from the inner policy's actions, reducing the risk of unstable learning by limiting the number of decisions made. To further improve performance, ProxPollo incorporates a technique that simulates the inner policy's actions in a more stable environment, providing a more accurate target for policy learning. In experiments, ProxPollo outperformed existing methods in various unstable environments and games, demonstrating its effectiveness and versatility. Additionally, we've shown that ProxPollo can learn quickly and efficiently in unstable environments, making it a reliable choice for a wide range of reinforcement learning tasks. This algorithm can be applied to a variety of applications, including continuous control, robotics, and adversarial games, and is expected to be a valuable addition to the field of reinforcement learning. We examine a distributed computing scenario where a network of interconnected nodes strives to achieve a shared goal, despite the presence of malicious actors within the network. These malicious actors, disguised as legitimate nodes, attempt to manipulate the computation to align with their own interests. We address this issue by developing a secure, distributed computation protocol that effectively counters the malicious behavior. This protocol leverages a property called linear separability, which is inherent in multiple significant computational problems. By utilizing a shared secret among the legitimate nodes and incorporating techniques from secret sharing, the protocol ensures the exclusion of malicious actors from the computation process. We further investigate the potential of this protocol to withstand even more severe security threats, where a substantial portion of the network, possibly exceeding half, consists of malicious actors. By incorporating advanced cryptographic methods, the protocol achieves robustness against these heightened security threats. This study provides a comprehensive framework for secure distributed computation, encompassing a diverse range of problems, including linearly separable problems, distributed computing, and multi-party secure encryption. As such, the proposed protocol holds significant value in multiple practical contexts, including data analysis and optimization. This work also contributes to the broader field of cryptography, specifically in the areas of multi-party computations and secure colorings, thereby highlighting its distinct contributions to the field. Finally, the proposed protocol has been rigorously tested and proven secure against even the most severe security threats. This security has been formally validated through a formal verification process. Additionally, the proposed protocol has been demonstrated to be efficient in terms of computational complexity and communication costs. Cosmological N-body simulations are a crucial tool for understanding the cosmic structure formation process. However, running these simulations is computationally expensive, and it's a challenging task to fine-tune parameters that can optimize simulation efficiency using gradient-based optimization techniques. To address this, we have developed a novel approach to calculating gradients for N-body simulations in a differentiable manner. Our method employs the adjoint method, which analytically computes the gradient of a desired outcome, while introducing a auxiliary variable and a backward simulation in conjunction. This allows us to perform gradient optimization for a variety of objectives, including accelerating simulations, improving mass assignment, and reconstructing initial conditions. Our approach is demonstrated through a series of experiments, which show that it successfully computes gradients in a computationally efficient manner. Additionally, we have successfully applied this method to a real-world scenario, where we utilized it to optimize a time-stepping parameter in a simulation. This resulted in a significant improvement in accuracy, as measured by the power spectrum. Our approach is made available as open-source software on GitHub. We envision that this method will enable future research into the theoretical and practical aspects of cosmological N-body simulations. The accompanying code can be found at: https://github.com/ImNeXuW/adjoint-nbody-simulation. The Bitcoin protocol offers an opportunity to link the potential advantages of quantum computing with the classical financial system. This interaction is facilitated by the non-deterministic nature of quantum mechanics, which could give quantum computers an unfair advantage in solving computational challenges for the benefit of cryptocurrency miners. As a result, miners would invest in the development of quantum computers to expedite Bitcoin mining. This note examines the conditions under which quantum computing can provide a real advantage in solving Bitcoin mining problems, revealing that current financial incentives for quantum computing primarily stem from the pursuit of numerical calculations rather than the potential financial returns associated with cryptocurrency. Nevertheless, we also identify a potential future connection between quantum computing and the world of cryptocurrency. Additionally, we explore the possibility of utilizing advanced classical algorithms to speed up the mining process, and demonstrate that these alternatives are often less efficient than the use of quantum computers. Finally, we outline a set of necessary conditions for quantum advantage in Bitcoin mining and suggest a novel quantum-classical mining model that could potentially lead to significant financial rewards for miners. An implementation of this new model is feasible with current quantum devices and can provide a notable financial advantage for cryptocurrency miners. Keywords: Quantum advantage, Bitcoin mining, quantum-classical computing, non-determinism, quantum economics. Pub-ID: arXiv:2206.01873. The evolution of interstellar matter plays a crucial role in shaping galaxy development.  Despite numerous studies, the process of interstellar matter enrichment remains poorly understood due to the scarcity of reliable data on metal content in galaxies at early cosmic epochs.  A recent study of 15 distant galaxies at z=5-9 has revealed that interstellar matter within these galaxies contains a higher concentration of metals compared to prior research.  Specifically, the study found that interstellar matter contains a median metal content of around 0.65 times the solar value, indicating a significant increase in metal concentration at z>4.  This finding is consistent with the rapid growth of star formation at early cosmic epochs.  Furthermore, the study's results suggest that interstellar matter within these galaxies is predominantly composed of metals produced by massive star explosions, rather than material ejected by older stars.  This suggests that supernovae have been the primary contributors to the enrichment of interstellar matter at z>4.  This finding is also supported by the detection of interstellar winds in some of these distant galaxies. In medical imaging analysis, the task of multi-modal brain tumor segmentation (MBS) aims to classify tumor regions within brain MR images. Current approaches typically combine features from various modalities using a specific fusion method, but these methods often fall short in accurately capturing the spatial correlations within and between tumor regions and image modalities. To address this limitation, a new method called MMsynFus is proposed, which first learns to generate missing modalities from available ones and then employs modality-level attention to effectively integrate the diverse modalities. By employing this method, MMsynFus is able to uncover spatial correlations within and between tumor regions and image modalities, leading to enhanced segmentation accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate that MMsynFus outperforms other methods in two prominent brain tumor segmentation challenges, BraTS2018 and BraTS2019. Notably, MMsynFus achieves the best public ranking in BraTS2019 and significantly improves the dice score for the whole tumor (57.46 to 58.69) and tumor core (49.46 to 51.69) segments. In MPLS networks, where traffic is routed through multiple layers, it can be difficult to track the path of actual data packets. Current methods for uncovering the path of these packets, known as "traceroute," rely on sending customized packets and analyzing responses. However, traditional approaches may not be effective in certain low-traffic network situations, leading researchers to explore an alternative approach. This new approach, known as TNT, sends data packets with unique identifiers and uses specialized network analysis tools to gather information. By continuously sending data, it can gather detailed insights into a network's behavior, effectively "shining a light" on the path it takes. This approach has been tested and shown to be capable of tracing network paths in various complex scenarios, even in situations where traditional methods fall short. Additionally, TNT has been found to be resistant to network interference and provides detailed insights into a network's behavior, which can be used to inform and improve network performance. This study compares various machine learning methods for determining the optimal system parameters of photonic circuits, specifically those using a Mach-Zehnder interferometer structure. To evaluate these methods, we utilize a high-level photonic simulation tool and apply them to an integrated photonic device that mimics the functionality of a matrix multiplier commonly used in neural network applications. Our experiments demonstrate that a simple genetic algorithm yields results comparable to more complex gradient-based methods such as backpropagation and Adam. Furthermore, we found that these techniques outperform human-designed system parameters in terms of key performance metrics, specifically the achieved neural network accuracy. Notably, a genetic algorithm achieves comparable results while requiring significantly fewer training iterations compared to gradient-based methods. These findings suggest that a genetic algorithm is a more efficient training tool for integrated photonic devices. Additionally, we found that incorporating a Z-score normalization step enhances the training process and enables the achievement of superior system parameters. Finally, we highlight the importance of incorporating a phase shifter model in the simulation framework to achieve the best possible system parameters. Specifically, omitting this model leads to suboptimal results, underscoring the significance of its inclusion for accurate device training. To facilitate further research, we provide open-source code for integrating the high-level photonic simulation tool with machine learning algorithms. Specifically, our code is available at https://github.com/jjfairley/mzr-sim and includes a simple implementation of the gradient-based method, which can be easily modified to accommodate other machine learning algorithms. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive tutorial on integrating our simulation tool with a genetic algorithm-based training agent, which can be accessed at https://github.com/jjfairley/mzr-fairley. In contrast, the code for the Adam-based training agent is proprietary and not included in our public repository. However, we do offer a custom version of our training agent for the PIC community, which can be accessed at https://github.com/jjfairley/mzr-fairley. In addition, we provide a detailed tutorial on integrating our simulation tool with a neural network-based training agent, which can be accessed at https://github.com/jjfairley/mzr-fairley. In summary, our study demonstrates the superiority of a genetic algorithm-based training agent for integrated photonic devices, the importance of including a phase shifter model, and highlights the potential for machine learning-based optimization techniques to achieve the best possible system parameters. Finally, we emphasize the significance of our simulation tool, which enables the training of integrated photonic devices.

The movement of the center of mass within a bag model is investigated. In the process, an effective potential is developed that simulates how the center of mass interacts with itself due to internal forces within the bag. Solving the Schrödinger equation with this potential reveals that the center of mass in a moving bag model exhibits a bound state. Furthermore, the binding energy is computable and conditional upon both mass and bag radius. In a specific case where the mass of the bag is equivalent to that of a nucleon, the binding energy is approximately 139.8 MeV. Notably, this binding energy is comparable to the binding energy of quarks within a nucleon. Consequently, it is hypothesized that the center of mass motion within a bag model could be a plausible explanation for the origin of quark masses. In related research, this hypothesis is to be verified through direct observation of center of mass motion within a nucleon. In addition, the potential also allows for the examination of how the center of mass moves within larger hadronic systems, such as bag models containing multiple nucleons. We explore the local Hamiltonian problem within a parameterized framework. Specifically, we consider weighted instances of this problem, where each qubit in a k-qubit system can have any of two states. Our investigation involves the parameterized complexity of the local Hamiltonian problem, where we analyze its complexity under various measures, including the standard measure, the quantum parameter measure, and the classical measures. Our research reveals that the weighted local Hamiltonian problem is equivalent to the quantum local Hamiltonian problem in terms of quantum parameter complexity but exhibits different complexity characteristics under classical measures, demonstrating its completeness under the z-measure, yet remaining in P for the t-measure. The widespread dissemination of misinformation has become a major concern, with many researchers attempting to develop effective methods to mitigate its impact on social media platforms. A crucial factor in mitigating misinformation spread is the way it interacts with existing social connections, with individuals being more resistant to opposing viewpoints within their social circle. Building on this concept, this study presents innovative approaches to depolarise social networks, with the primary goal of increasing exposure to opposing viewpoints, while also addressing the risk of a backfire effect, where previously accepted information unexpectedly contradicts one's beliefs. The authors examine two scenarios: one in which individuals can be encouraged to engage in online discussions and another where existing network connections can be manipulated. The resulting methods are evaluated on both theoretical and practical grounds, with the theoretical framework providing a fundamental limit on achievable outcomes and simulation results demonstrating the practical feasibility of these methods. Ultimately, this study contributes meaningfully to existing research on mitigating misinformation spread by accounting for the complex dynamics of social connections and the psychological impact of conflicting information. A crucial test for Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) is their ability to accurately solve complex ordinary differential equations (ODEs). Evaluating these equations, especially when highly nonlinear and interconnected, poses significant challenges and showcases the potential of PINNs to provide approximate solutions. To create a reliable benchmark system for evaluating the accuracy of PINNs in solving ODEs, we developed a set of solvable ODE systems that vary in difficulty and non-linearity. These systems are designed to test the capabilities of PINNs in solving complex problems, with a focus on how increased non-linearity and interdependence between variables impact their performance. By applying PINNs to our carefully crafted benchmark systems, we found that even with high non-linearity and interdependence, multiple hidden layers in PINNs can still achieve high accuracy. Furthermore, we demonstrated that the accuracy of PINNs can be further improved by adjusting key parameters such as the number of training data points, hidden units, layers, and activation functions. Our findings highlight the importance of carefully designing test problems to evaluate the strengths and limitations of PINNs. With these optimized parameters, we found that PINNs can solve challenging ODE systems with high non-linearity and interdependence, even when only a limited number of training data points are available. Overall, our work provides valuable insights into how to develop reliable and efficient methods for solving ODEs using PINNs. We introduce a innovative, multi-purpose manipulation technique for flexible materials, which we call Canonicalized-Alignment (CanCan). This method involves initially flattening the cloth and then aligning its principal axes with the arm's surface normal and axis. CanCan serves as a versatile prior for a range of manipulation tasks and can be integrated with various control methods to improve their performance. When paired with a basic motion planner, CanCan yields high-quality manipulation trajectories that outperform current methods built on traditional cloth solvers, while also streamlining the design and training of learning-based controllers. CanCan's versatility is demonstrated across a variety of tasks including cloth folding, packing, and packing-and-folding, highlighting its potential as a universal, efficient, and learnable prior for a range of flexible manipulation tasks. Neutrinos play a crucial role in understanding the evolution of neutron star mergers.  Neutrinos' complex behavior can be calculated by solving the Boltzmann equation, which can be simplified to assess instability caused by flavor oscillations using specific metrics.  This work evaluates the accuracy of such metrics in a simplified model of a neutron star merger, comparing them to the actual behavior calculated from the Boltzmann equation.  Results show that while these metrics provide a good approximation for large oscillation amplitudes, they significantly underestimate the actual behavior for smaller amplitudes, and their predictions diverge as the simulation advances.  This finding has implications for using these metrics to infer properties of neutron stars or to detect gravitational waves, highlighting the need for a more accurate approach.  A revised metric is proposed to improve estimation for small oscillation amplitudes, and its performance is demonstrated in a neutron star merger scenario.  This work provides a foundation for future research to develop more accurate metrics for understanding neutrino behavior in such complex astrophysical events. Open-set recognition is a challenging task in its field, aiming to identify instances that don't belong to any known class. Conventional methods typically create a metric space using pre-trained model features, but this approach is flawed as it may fail to generalize effectively due to training data limitations and a lack of diversity. To overcome these issues, we introduce an open-set recognition framework centered around similarity learning. Our approach leverages a variety of image transformations, such as color palette and lighting changes, to significantly expand the pool of available features and improve its capacity for generalization. Additionally, we propose a novel similarity metric that incorporates feature embeddings from both the input class and a diverse set of reference classes. Our experiments demonstrate that this framework excels in open-set recognition, surpassing state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks.
